steps.title: Đọc
steps.heading: What makes a claim compelling?
steps.purpose: Đọc để tìm: một lập luận mạnh cần những yếu tố nào, và tác giả minh hoạ bằng ví dụ gì?
text: Every serious argument begins with a claim, and the claim about automation could hardly be more contested. Some economists argue that machines will create more work than they remove; others maintain that the transition will leave millions of people behind. There is no denying that both camps can point to evidence, yet it is the quality of the reasoning, not the volume of the assertion, that decides which case deserves to be taken seriously.

Consider what a strong claim actually requires. What distinguishes a persuasive writer from a merely confident one is precision: the claim is specific, it can be tested, and it admits its own limits. To say that automation is good or bad is to say almost nothing. To argue that automation will accelerate job displacement in routine clerical roles within a decade is to make a statement that evidence can support or undermine.

The labour market offers a compelling case study. It is the mismatch between available vacancies and available skills that explains why unemployment can persist while employers complain of shortages. The reason why a skills gap matters so much is that it turns an abstract forecast into a personal problem. A worker made redundant in logistics gains nothing from a surplus of posts in data science unless a route between the two exists.

A compelling case, in other words, is built from three elements. First comes a clear claim; second, a reason that connects the claim to the problem; and third, evidence that a sceptical reader could check. It is only when all three are present that an argument moves from opinion to analysis. Writers who maintain that technology will solve its own problems, without showing how, offer an assertion rather than an argument, and readers are right to withhold their agreement.

box.title: Ghi nhớ: câu chẻ và pseudo-cleft
box.intro: Câu chẻ tách câu thường thành hai mệnh đề để nhấn mạnh một thành phần (chủ ngữ, tân ngữ, trạng ngữ, lý do).

text: A claim without evidence is merely an opinion, and the strongest writers know it. According to the World Economic Forum, roughly 22 per cent of today's jobs will be disrupted by 2030, with 170 million roles created and 92 million displaced. What these figures show is not a verdict but a direction: the labour market is being reorganised, and the net result depends on who is able to move. Evidence, however, is never self-explanatory; it has to be interpreted.

A growing body of evidence suggests that the gains and the losses fall on different people. McKinsey's analysis of the United States estimates that up to 30 per cent of the hours worked could be automated by 2030. It also finds that the lowest-paid workers are up to fourteen times more likely to need to change occupation than the best paid. It is not the average that should concern policymakers, but the distribution around it.

A case in point is the gig economy. Platforms can boost productivity by matching tasks with workers in a matter of minutes, and many users value the flexibility. Yet the same arrangement shifts risk from the firm to the individual, which is why the model is often described as a double-edged sword. What a single statistic can never reveal is how a worker experiences that risk on an ordinary Tuesday.

Good writers therefore treat evidence with care. They cite the source, state the date, and say what the figure does and does not prove. It is by reporting the limits honestly that a writer earns the reader's trust, and it is that trust, far more than any single statistic, that makes an argument persuasive. A careless citation does more harm than silence.

steps.title: Nghe
text: A claim without evidence is merely an opinion, and the strongest writers know it. According to the World Economic Forum, roughly 22 per cent of today's jobs will be disrupted by 2030, with 170 million roles created and 92 million displaced. What these figures show is not a verdict but a direction: the labour market is being reorganised, and the net result depends on who is able to move. Evidence, however, is never self-explanatory; it has to be interpreted.

A growing body of evidence suggests that the gains and the losses fall on different people. McKinsey's analysis of the United States estimates that up to 30 per cent of the hours worked could be automated by 2030. It also finds that the lowest-paid workers are up to fourteen times more likely to need to change occupation than the best paid. It is not the average that should concern policymakers, but the distribution around it.

A case in point is the gig economy. Platforms can boost productivity by matching tasks with workers in a matter of minutes, and many users value the flexibility. Yet the same arrangement shifts risk from the firm to the individual, which is why the model is often described as a double-edged sword. What a single statistic can never reveal is how a worker experiences that risk on an ordinary Tuesday.

Good writers therefore treat evidence with care. They cite the source, state the date, and say what the figure does and does not prove. It is by reporting the limits honestly that a writer earns the reader's trust, and it is that trust, far more than any single statistic, that makes an argument persuasive. A careless citation does more harm than silence.

steps.title: Đọc
steps.heading: The art of persuasion
steps.purpose: Đọc để tìm: người thuyết phục hiệu quả kết hợp những yếu tố nào, và vì sao câu chuyện cụ thể lại có sức mạnh?
text: Persuasion is not the same as proof. A speaker may hold the better evidence and still lose the room if the audience feels unaddressed. Effective advocates therefore appeal to values as well as to facts: they ask what listeners fear, what they hope for, and what they are prepared to defend. What turns a statistic into a call to action is the story attached to it. Neither statistics nor stories are sufficient on their own, and a speaker who offers only one of them is half prepared.

Those who call for stronger protection for displaced workers rarely rely on data alone. They describe the machinist of fifty-two who has lost a post he held for thirty years, and they let the audience supply the conclusion. It is this concrete detail that can sway opinion where an abstract percentage would not. Critics of the tactic point out that emotion can mislead, and they are right to do so; but the answer is balance, not abstinence.

Consider the debate about inequality. Campaigners who advocate retraining programmes argue that failing to act will widen the inequality gap and erode job security for millions. To rally support, they link the issue to something every voter understands: the fear that one's own children will inherit a more precarious working life. The reason why this works is that it converts a systemic problem into a personal stake.

To take a stand is a risk, because a clear position invites disagreement. Yet audiences distrust speakers who hedge on everything. What persuades in the end is a combination of credibility, clarity and courage. It is the willingness to say what should be done, and to explain why workers must reskill, employers must invest and governments must pay for the transition.

steps.heading: Should robots pay taxes?
steps.purpose: Đọc một bài mới dùng lại các cụm của tuần: tác giả trình bày hai phía thế nào?
text: Few proposals divide opinion as sharply as the idea of taxing robots. Supporters argue that firms which replace workers with machines should contribute to the cost of the transition. They maintain that without such a levy the burden will fall on those least able to bear it. There is no denying that the idea has intuitive appeal, but intuition is not evidence.

According to critics, a robot tax would penalise exactly the investment that could boost productivity. What they fear is that firms would simply delay modernisation, leaving the labour market weaker and wages stagnant. A growing body of evidence from countries with high levels of automation suggests that productivity gains and employment can rise together, although the gains are rarely shared evenly.

Advocates respond that the question is not whether to tax automation but how to fund the reskilling that it makes necessary. They call for a modest, transparent charge directed towards lifelong learning, and they appeal to fairness rather than to hostility towards technology. A case in point is a scheme in which firms that displace staff contribute to training funds, an arrangement that can rally support among workers without alienating investors.

It is unlikely that either side will win outright. Neither camp can afford to ignore the other's strongest point. What matters is that the debate is conducted with precision about what is being claimed, what evidence supports it, and what would count as failure. Governments that strike a balance between encouraging innovation and protecting workers will be better placed to mitigate the impact of change. Those that take a stand on principle rather than slogan will sway opinion more durably than those that merely shout without offering any alternative.

steps.heading: Rebutting (preview)
steps.purpose: Đọc lướt để làm quen với tuần sau: cách phản bác một lập luận.
text: Every claim invites a reply. A careful writer will not simply dismiss the claim of an opponent but will counter the argument with evidence. To some extent, critics of automation are right that jobs are at risk; yet a focus on losses alone is beside the point if the real question is how to respond. On the contrary, the evidence suggests that societies which invest in lifelong learning, strike a balance and mitigate the impact of change fare better.

steps.title: Tự viết có hẹn giờ
steps.prompt: Timed writing (12 minutes): write a short essay of 170 to 200 words on this claim: "Governments should call for stronger protection for workers displaced by automation." State your position, give a reason and evidence, concede one opposing point (to some extent), and rebut it. Use at least one cleft sentence.
steps.hint: Position, reason, evidence, concession, rebuttal, conclusion.
steps.sample: Governments should call for stronger protection for workers displaced by automation, because the costs of change fall on those least able to bear them.
steps.model:
Governments should call for stronger protection for workers displaced by automation, because the costs of change fall on those least able to bear them. According to McKinsey, the lowest-paid workers are up to fourteen times more likely to need to change occupation than the best paid. What makes this alarming is that these are the people with the fewest savings and the least time to retrain.

Critics argue that stronger protection would discourage firms from innovating. To some extent, this concern is justified: poorly designed rules can raise costs and delay modernisation. Yet it is the design of the protection, not its existence, that determines its effect. A transparent training fund, financed by firms that displace staff, would support lifelong learning without penalising investment.

There is no denying that technology will continue to reshape the labour market. The reason why protection matters is that it allows societies to share the gains and mitigate the impact of change. Governments that strike a balance between innovation and fairness will keep both, and a society is ultimately judged by how it treats the people its machines replace.
